WEREWOLF

A better game night.

the idea

Werewolf started with a practical question in my high school dorm: could the host deal and remember secret roles without getting in the way of the game?

Evolving project · selected interface explorations
The project

Game experience & web development

My focus

Product decisions, interface iteration & AI-assisted development

At a glance

Private role reveals · Room-based play · Repeated rounds

The situation

Let the table
focus on the game.

In the dorm, Werewolf brings people around the same table. The host still has to keep track of the room, distribute identities, and help everyone move into a new round.

I built the tool with AI as a collaborator, shaping the requirements, interface decisions, and iterations around that shared experience.

The experience

One shared room.
One private identity.

A room code gives everyone a common starting point. Configuration belongs to the host; each player sees their own role. That distinction is central to the experience.

Keeping a room available across rounds makes a game night feel continuous, while the interface keeps the current game and its actions legible.

Exploring privacy

A secret should stay
a deliberate reveal.

A later local player-card exploration starts with a neutral card. The player chooses when to reveal a role and can hide it again.

The mobile exploration also separates reading a long role description from changing cards. These screens show local design work, rather than a claim about the current live version.

What stays with me

A project lives
with its people.

Sharing updates in the dorm and collecting suggestions made the work a continuing conversation. The site grew from dealing identities toward supporting the rhythm of a game night.

The most useful decisions were often about attention: what the host needs now, what a player should see privately, and what can wait.
